narrative:
The model estimates a 60% chance that you will leave, meaning leaving is considered more likely than staying. Because a promotion is a longer-term investment, that elevated risk is why the promotion is being denied at this time.

The strongest signal pushing toward leaving was your total experience of 6–10 years. Among employees predicted to stay, only about 35% have this level of experience, while half have 1–5 years, so your profile sits further along the career timeline where movement becomes more likely. The next strongest signal was your 1–5 years in the current organization; although this is the most common range among employees predicted to stay, in your profile it still added to the leave signal. The third signal, having no other job opportunities, worked in the opposite direction: it lowered the predicted risk, since most employees predicted to stay also report no outside opportunities. Even so, it was not enough to offset the experience-related signals.

Before revisiting promotion, the organization should discuss your career path, retention and progression, and what would make staying attractive. You should clarify what development, support or role change would address the factors that may be making you a flight risk.
